lines.text: On every public trading venue, your order is visible before it fills. A bot reads the size, buys ahead of you, and sells into your fill. You pay for the privilege of being seen. This is dorr — perpetual futures on Flare, where the venue matching your order cannot read it.

That number is not marketing copy. This page just ran the attack against the live pool. On a transparent exchange a front-runner took two hundred and five dollars out of this order. Here it takes nothing.
The mechanism is four steps, and the first happens before anything leaves your machine. Your order is timelock-encrypted in the browser to a drand round that has not been published yet.
So what the operator receives is ciphertext and a thirty-two byte commitment. Not a promise that it will not look — the decryption key does not exist yet, anywhere.
When the round lands, every order in that epoch clears at a single uniform price. A bot that front-runs and back-runs is buying and selling at the same number.
And the chain checks our arithmetic. The settlement contract re-reads FTSO version two itself and reverts if our clearing price is off-market. The referee is Flare, not us.
Rather than describe that, let's attack it. This is a real sandwich against the live virtual AMM — real fills, real reserves, restored afterwards.

On the transparent side the bot spots the order in the clear, front-runs it, and pockets two hundred and five dollars. On dorr it sees a hash. It tries twenty-five thousand real SHA-256 preimages, gets zero matches, and aborts. The victim fills at the fair price.
The sealing uses a live drand round from the League of Entropy — a twelve of twenty-two threshold network. Watch the operator try to decrypt early and get refused.
And under uniform-price clearing the sandwich nets exactly zero. Not because we forbid it. Because both legs execute at the same price.
Same order, two venues, side by side. The only variable is the market design.
Now let's actually use it. Connecting a wallet on Flare Coston2. That balance is a real read from the vault contract, not a number this page invented.
Collateral is FXRP — Flare's FAssets bridged XRP. Balance, free, and locked, read straight from the vault address shown underneath.
Testnet FXRP comes from the FAssets faucet. Real bridged asset mechanics, no value at stake.
Margin and leverage. Notional and the liquidation distance recompute against the live FTSO mark price as you move them.
And this is the switch that matters. Private: the public sees only a hash. Public foil: your full order is broadcast, the way every other venue works. Same engine, one flag.
Signing the order now. A real EIP-191 signature, bound to these exact parameters, submitted on-chain to Flare Coston2.
And here is the whole claim in one panel. The public feed shows a hash. No side, no size, no price, no leverage. That is everything an observer gets, including the operator.
The same order, from the side that owns it. Entry, mark, liquidation price, margin — visible to you, opaque to everyone else.
On the Coston2 explorer: a batch settling on-chain. The logs carry the epoch, the membership root and the clearing price the contract checked against the oracle.
And the vault's own transaction list. Deposits in, depositor-signed withdrawals out, and nothing from the operator, because there is nothing it could send.

This page is read live from the running system. The contracts come from the operator, the attestation from the enclave itself. Nothing here is typed by hand — if the page and the deployment ever disagree, the page is wrong.

Hardware attestation is live. The matching engine runs inside a Phala confidential VM on Intel TDX, and the operator holds no attestation key at all — it delegates, so it cannot forge a quote even for itself.
This is the raw attestation. Five thousand and ten bytes of Intel TDX quote, a version four header, and a quote hash you can check against the machine's own attestation page.

And this is the field that matters. Report data is the batch payload hash. The CPU signature covers this specific settlement — not merely the fact that an enclave was running somewhere. For contrast, the closest competing entry reports an image digest from an environment variable the container sets about itself, and never fetches a quote at all.

What is not proven. Version one runs a trusted operator for matching and execution, like a sequencer. Liquidity is a virtual AMM, not an external order book. It is testnet, and it is unaudited. Those are real limits and we would rather state them than have you find them.

Every contract address, every transaction hash and the live attestation are in the repository and on the verify page, so you can check any of this yourself rather than take our word for it. Thanks very much for watching.
